messages.subject: question on mirtCAT
parts:
Hello Phil,

I would like to do multidimensional CAT (MCAT) simulations. I have already fitted a MIRT model on my data (9-factor model with correlated factors), estimated individuals thetas (or IRT scores which will be considered as my "true scores" to compare with the MCAT scores). I want to use a "real data" simulation approach, i.e use the observed item responses rather than use simulated patterns. To use the mirtCAT function it requires complete responses patterns. So is it necessary to impute the missing responses ? Can I simply perform the MCAT using only the complete ones ? Or is there another way to do ?

I have another question: what is the best method to transform the IRT scores into score on a 0-100 scale score ? I was thinking about a inverse-logit transformation, but the results are quite strange when I check some isolated observations (e.g. an individual who responds the maximal category on all items doesn't have necessarily the maximal score). Is it an effect of the factor intercorrelations ?

Thank you for your consideration,

Pierre

parts: Hi Pierre,

On Thu, Feb 26, 2015 at 8:50 AM, Pierre Michel <aliasj...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hello Phil,

I would like to do multidimensional CAT (MCAT) simulations. I have already fitted a MIRT model on my data (9-factor model with correlated factors), estimated individuals thetas (or IRT scores which will be considered as my "true scores" to compare with the MCAT scores). I want to use a "real data" simulation approach, i.e use the observed item responses rather than use simulated patterns. To use the mirtCAT function it requires complete responses patterns. So is it necessary to impute the missing responses ? Can I simply perform the MCAT using only the complete ones ? Or is there another way to do ?

I'm not sure I understand what you mean here. Each person was given a test, but the test was smaller for each individual than the total number of items, and therefore NA's should be used for items that were not observed. Now, you wish to pass these observed responses into a CAT? That doesn't make sense to me. What if an item is selected during the CAT where no observed response was realized (i.e., it turns out they have high ability, so a difficult item is selected, for which they originally did not respond to). That sorta blows the whole point of CAT out of the water, unless I'm missing something....

I have another question: what is the best method to transform the IRT scores into score on a 0-100 scale score ? I was thinking about a inverse-logit transformation, but the results are quite strange when I check some isolated observations (e.g. an individual who responds the maximal category on all items doesn't have necessarily the maximal score). Is it an effect of the factor intercorrelations ?

I'm not really sure I understand this either. You can scale the scores using the standard transformation formula score = mu + sd*z, but bounding them between 0 and 100 is a little trickier, which is why companies like ETS generally don't do that (they usually set things to have a mean of something like 500, SD = 100, which generally avoids flooring affects). Perhaps something like a truncated normal would do, but I would advise against it. Cheers.

Phil

Thank you for your consideration,

Pierre

For simulations, you shouldn't be using previous response patterns anyway. Simulation evaluations are about determining how hypothetical individuals should respond in the CAT, and seeing how well population characteristics can be recovered. For observed individuals, population characteristics are not known anyway, and therefore don't add much.

I have another question: what is the best method to transform the IRT scores into score on a 0-100 scale score ? Anyway, is it normal to observe big differences between IRT scores and mean raw scores ? That's why I suppose there is an effect of the factor correlations on the latent traits estimations...

I would still advise against that, because it seems to be about reference scoring rather than an invertible transformation (and depends on how variable your population is, as well as what estimators were used). The theta's are already in a linear and unbounded metric, so that property should be preserved. And yes, total scores can be very different from IRT scores, because the latter is based on a 0 centered metric (hence, shifts with the difficulty of the test). 

Phil

I see that, but I really wonder what use it could be to understanding the bank as a whole. If you really insist on doing this, here's the steps:

- Each person essentially gets their own 'customized item bank'. Rather than building 1 full CAT with all items, build a mirt object using only the observed items for that particular person using the population IRT parameters 
- Using the complete data response vector (extracted out manually, so no NA's should be present) pass this to local.pattern instead of the full response with a mixture of NAs and responses
- Adjust whatever properties you like for the CAT to see how things would have behaved
- Repeat for all individuals, building a customized CAT for each person

That should accomplish your goal, though admittedly it is a bit awkward (but then, the question is kind of awkward too, so I guess it fits). Cheers.

Phil

On Thu, Feb 26, 2015 at 1:59 PM, <aliasj...@gmail.com> wrote:
Among the different CAT simulations approches, There is one called post hoc simulation (or "real data" simulation). This is described on this link http://iacat.org/content/research-strategies-cat . It seems that the CAT procedures may be simulated using the available response data. 

Pierre MICHEL
